question: How many strings of length \(5\) formed from the digits \(0,\) \(1,\) \(2,\) \(3,\) \(4\) are there such that for each \(j\in\{1,2,3,4\},\) at least \(j\) of the digits are less than \(j?\) (For example, \(02214\) satisfies the condition because it contains at least \(1\) digit less than \(1,\) at least \(2\) digits less than \(2,\) at least \(3\) digits less than \(3,\) and at least \(4\) digits less than \(4.\) The string \(23404\) does not satisfy the condition because it does not contain at least \(2\) digits less than \(2.\))
solution:
Rearranging the digits does not change how many are less than any given number. We can first find the acceptable strings in sorted order, then count their distinct rearrangements.

Let the sorted digits be \(d_1\le d_2\le\cdots\le d_5\). Having at least \(j\) digits less than \(j\) means exactly that \(d_j<j\). Thus the restrictions are
\[
d_1=0,\qquad d_2\le1,\qquad d_3\le2,\qquad d_4\le3,\qquad d_5\le4.
\]
The last bound already holds because the allowed digits are \(0\) through \(4\).

To list all possibilities systematically, start with \(d_1=0\), then choose each \(d_i\) from \(d_{i-1}\) through \(i-1\). Group the resulting strings by their digit multiplicities. For example, pattern \((3,1,1)\) means that one digit occurs three times and two other digits occur once each.

| Multiplicities | Acceptable sorted strings | Number |
|---|---|---:|
| \((5)\) | \(00000\) | 1 |
| \((4,1)\) | \(00001,\ 00002,\ 00003,\ 00004,\ 01111\) | 5 |
| \((3,2)\) | \(00011,\ 00022,\ 00033,\ 00111,\ 00222\) | 5 |
| \((3,1,1)\) | \(00012,\ 00013,\ 00014,\ 00023,\ 00024,\ 00034,\ 01112,\ 01113,\ 01114,\ 01222\) | 10 |
| \((2,2,1)\) | \(00112,\ 00113,\ 00114,\ 00122,\ 00133,\ 00223,\ 00224,\ 00233,\ 01122,\ 01133\) | 10 |
| \((2,1,1,1)\) | \(00123,\ 00124,\ 00134,\ 00234,\ 01123,\ 01124,\ 01134,\ 01223,\ 01224,\ 01233\) | 10 |
| \((1,1,1,1,1)\) | \(01234\) | 1 |

These seven patterns cover every way that positive multiplicities can sum to \(5\). Within each row, the sorted-digit bounds give exactly the strings listed.

For multiplicities \(m_1,\ldots,m_r\), the number of distinct rearrangements is
\[
\frac{5!}{m_1!\cdots m_r!}.
\]
Indeed, temporarily distinguishing identical copies gives \(5!\) arrangements, but permuting the copies of any one digit does not change the actual string. For the seven rows, the rearrangement counts are respectively
\[
\frac{5!}{5!}=1,\quad
\frac{5!}{4!}=5,\quad
\frac{5!}{3!2!}=10,\quad
\frac{5!}{3!}=20,\quad
\frac{5!}{2!2!}=30,\quad
\frac{5!}{2!}=60,\quad
5!=120.
\]
Every string has a unique sorted form, so rearrangements from different listed forms cannot overlap. The total is therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
&1\cdot1+5\cdot5+5\cdot10+10\cdot20\\
&\qquad+10\cdot30+10\cdot60+1\cdot120\\
&=1+25+50+200+300+600+120\\
&=\boxed{1296}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The answer is choice \(\text{E}\).
